Hi Leah,

Appreciate the demand profile — good level of detail. High level up front: we usually recommend a mixed-pool approach for workloads like yours. Briefly:
- H100: prioritize long-context, memory-resident models (heavy KV cache) where model memory and NVLink bandwidth matter.
- A100: workhorse for high-throughput generation with good memory and throughput balance for 32–80B-class models.
- L4: cost-efficient for embeddings and cheap burst capacity; we use these as isolated pools for stateless, short-context inferencing.

Next steps I propose: 1) Connor will run a quick slot-level sizing using your token distributions and target p95s, 2) Marcus will scope operational headroom and thermal/placement constraints, 3) we'll deliver a one-page recommended mix and a reserve/burst split you can put into the SOW.

A few clarifying asks (quick):
- What percent of requests read from cache vs cold-start? (cache hit-rate assumption drives how much H100 memory you need)
- Do you have hard p99 SLOs? p95 targets are helpful but p99 planning materially affects headroom sizing.

We'll aim to get a draft sizing and a simple TCO table by EOD tomorrow.

Best,
Olga Petrov
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Leah / Olga,

Attached below is a concise run-through of the slot math and a recommended conservative mix. I used the demand profile and assumed: 65% cache hit-rate for long-context chat, average output tokens per request = 800, bulk embeddings qps sustained outside peak windows. Key notes:

1) Baseline compute assumptions (models & perf):
- Large chat model (memory-resident): logical memory ~120GB, single-token latency ~= 3.4ms on H100 under continuous batching; on A100 the same model needs sharding and shows ~4.8ms single-token latency.
- Throughput model (stateless generation / 32B): A100 achieves ~2.1K tokens/sec per GPU under 1ms preferrable latency window; L4 is ~350–500 tokens/sec optimized for short contexts (embeddings).

2) Headroom & reserve/burst:
- For your p95 targets and 2,400 spike tolerance, we recommend a reserve commit sized to cover 80% of expected sustained peak and a burst pool (on-demand) to cover the remaining 20% of spike capacity. That means an initial reserve ratio of 4:1 (reserve:bust slots) for predictable cost accounting.

3) Recommended slot mix (initial pilot -> production ramp):
- Pilot (month 0–3): 12 H100 slots, 28 A100 slots, 6 L4 slots. Rationale: H100 cover memory resident chat with KV cache, A100 handle steady high-throughput generation and fallback for mid-length chat, L4 for embeddings and cheap burst.
- Production(steady state): 18 H100, 64 A100, 20 L4 (scale A100 to handle baseline qps and reduce per-token unit cost).

4) Fallback/quantization strategy:
- Memory-bound requests routed to H100 first. When H100 utilization > 75% we route compatible requests to A100 with model quantization to int8 (tested accuracy delta ~0.6% on your eval set). L4 remains isolated for embeddings only to avoid tail-latency interference.

5) Ops & caching assumptions that drive sizing:
- If cache hit-rate drops below 50% we recommend +30% H100 headroom or reconfigure routing to increase A100 fallback.
- We assumed 5–10% reserved headroom for preemption/maintenance.

6) TCO note (ballpark):
- Cost-per-token optimized by shifting embeddings to L4 and scaling A100; H100 increases capex but reduces request-level latency and p99 variability for long-context traffic. We'll provide a model with token-dollar breakdown in the attached Redwood_SKU_TCO_Calc.xlsx.

If this readout looks good I'll fold into a short one-pager and a suggested clause we can include in the SOW about reserve/burst sizing and fallback policies.

Connor O'Brien
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Leah / team,

Operational callouts from infra:
- Provisioning lead time: H100 racks typically require a 6–8 week lead (scheduling + network fabric), A100 4–6 weeks, L4 (lighter footprint) 2–3 weeks. If you need a hard start date we recommend staging H100 earlier in the SOW.
- Thermal & placement: H100 density increases cooling load; recommend we reserve adjacent racks and a maintenance window for node replacement to avoid noisy-neighbor effects.
- Overcommit policy: we propose a slot-level overcommit of 1.15x for A100 only (to improve utilization) and strict 1.0x for H100 to preserve latency SLOs.

SLA implications: to meet the p95/p99 commitments above we should include explicit fallback policies (quantization + A100 fallback) and a documented failover route to hosted API in the SOW for catastrophic capacity events.

I can draft a short ops appendix to include in the SOW that lists provisioning lead times, maintenance windows, and the overcommit guardrails.

Marcus Lin
Head of Infrastructure Planning, Redwood Inference
